brief.student_must_understand: The wing has lower pressure above and higher pressure below; air spills around the tip, creating a vortex/downwash system associated with induced drag.
refine: Use one credible wing section/planform
Make the pressure-to-vortex cause-and-effect sequence obvious
Avoid wake-turbulence operational clutter

visuals.mapping_reason: Question 1178 asks what creates induced drag; the visual directly connects the top/bottom pressure difference to wingtip roll-up and the induced-drag consequence.

visuals.concept: The vertical fin aft of the CG provides directional/yaw stability by weather-vaning the aircraft back into the relative wind
visuals.reuse_justification: All four questions test the exact same relationship: the vertical fin provides directional stability in the yawing plane.

source.notes: Handbook states directional stability is accomplished by the vertical stabilizer/fin aft of the CG, acting like a weather vane; Figure 1-31 illustrates yaw control at the fin/rudder.

brief.student_must_understand: A yaw/sideslip exposes the vertical fin to relative airflow; the aerodynamic side force at the tail creates a restoring yaw moment toward the original direction.
refine: Use a clean top/three-quarter aircraft view
Separate stability function of fin from pilot rudder-control input
Make restoring moment obvious

visuals.mapping_reason: These questions all ask the same directional-stability relationship and the approved handbook directly explains the vertical fin weather-vane restoring action.

visuals.concept: The colour-coded ASI places VFE at the top of the white arc, VNO at the top of the green arc/start of yellow, and VNE at the red line
visuals.reuse_justification: All six questions test the same standard ASI limit geometry and operational meaning of VFE, VNO or VNE.

source.notes: Chapter 3 Airspeed Indicator Markings defines the white flap range and VFE upper limit, green normal range and VNO upper limit, yellow caution range, and red-line VNE.

brief.student_must_understand: Read VFE, VNO and VNE directly from one standard colour-coded ASI.
preserve: White, green and yellow arc order
refine: Use a clean credible light-aircraft ASI
Do not invent aircraft-specific speeds
Make the three limit boundaries unmistakable
add: Minimal VFE, VNO and VNE callouts

preserve: Low speed at surface versus faster outer flow
refine: Show a simple boundary-layer velocity gradient
Keep the wing/surface technically credible
Make the contact mechanism obvious

visuals.concept: In level flight, lower speed requires higher AoA and therefore greater induced drag
visuals.reuse_justification: All five questions test the same chain: speed down -> required AoA up -> induced drag up, or equivalently AoA up -> induced drag up.

source.notes: The induced-drag section states induced drag rises with AoA and when the airplane is flown slower; Figure 1-15 shows induced drag high at low speed and decreasing with speed.

brief.student_must_understand: Low speed in level flight requires higher AoA, so induced drag is high; higher speed lowers required AoA and induced drag.
preserve: Induced-drag curve high at low speed
Low speed linked to higher required AoA
refine: Use one simple speed-versus-induced-drag curve plus two wing-AoA states
Keep axes unambiguous
Avoid unrelated total/parasite drag clutter

visuals.mapping_reason: The questions directly test induced drag increasing with lower speed or greater AoA, including total drag below best L/D.

visuals.concept: Higher altitude, temperature and humidity reduce density; lower density degrades lift/propulsive performance, lengthens take-off and reduces climb
visuals.reuse_justification: These questions test branches of the same density-performance chain: temperature, pressure/altitude and water-vapour content determine density and reduced density degrades performance.

source.notes: Figure 1-17 and text connect altitude, temperature and humidity to density, take-off run and rate of climb; warm and humid air are less dense and lower density reduces performance.

brief.student_must_understand: Hotter, higher and more humid conditions reduce density; lower density means poorer performance, longer take-off and weaker climb.
preserve: Altitude, temperature and humidity as separate drivers
All arrows lead to lower density
refine: Use a clean cause-effect flow, not generic weather art
Make density the central physical link
Use one credible take-off/climb cue

visuals.mapping_reason: The questions test how temperature, humidity and atmospheric properties affect density and aircraft lift/performance.

visuals.concept: The down-going aileron increases local AoA/lift and induced drag, yawing the nose opposite the intended roll unless coordinated with rudder
visuals.reuse_justification: All three questions test the same adverse-yaw mechanism: extra induced drag on the down-going-aileron wing causes initial yaw opposite roll and same-direction rudder coordinates it.

source.notes: Figure 1-30 establishes that lowering an aileron increases local AoA and lift. The induced-drag section on page 1-8 establishes greater AoA/lift produces greater induced drag; together with the exact exam relationship this yields adverse yaw.

brief.student_must_understand: For a left roll the right aileron goes down, gains lift and drag, so the nose initially yaws right; left rudder coordinates the roll.
preserve: More lift/drag on down-going right aileron
refine: Use a top/rear view where roll and yaw cannot be confused
Show drag asymmetry without exaggerated vortices
Keep rudder correction secondary to cause
add: More induced drag on right wing

visuals.mapping_reason: The questions ask the direction/cause of adverse aileron yaw and its rudder correction; the visual isolates the drag asymmetry that causes it.

visuals.concept: A balance tab moves opposite the primary control surface so its aerodynamic force assists surface movement and reduces pilot control force
visuals.reuse_justification: All seven questions test the same balance-tab relationship: the tab deflects opposite the attached primary surface and thereby provides aerodynamic assistance that reduces control force.

source.notes: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 6, states that balance tabs automatically move opposite the main control surface; the resulting airflow counterbalances pressure on the main surface and reduces the force needed to move it.

brief.student_must_understand: When the elevator, rudder, or aileron moves one way, its balance tab moves the opposite way; airflow on the tab helps move the main surface instead of adding pilot effort.
preserve: Tab motion opposite the primary surface
Tab mounted at the primary surface trailing edge
Aerodynamic assistance in the direction of commanded primary-surface movement
refine: Use one credible generic control-surface section rather than three separate aircraft controls
Make the two opposite deflections immediately readable
Separate the movement relationship from the resulting assistance

visuals.mapping_reason: These questions ask either the relative movement or force-reducing purpose of a balance tab; one opposite-deflection teaching visual directly explains both parts of that exact mechanism.

visual_inspection.review_note: The exact optimized 1600x1050 PNG and matching WebP were rendered and inspected against the locked Batch 1 quality standard. The primary surface and trailing-edge balance tab move in unmistakably opposite directions, while the airflow-assistance cue and reduced-pilot-force outcome remain distinct and readable. An ambiguous extra motion arrow was removed before approval.

visuals.concept: An anti-servo tab moves in the same direction as the stabilator, increasing aerodynamic resistance and control feel so the all-moving tail is less sensitive
visuals.reuse_justification: All four questions test the identical anti-balance/anti-servo preflight relationship: the tab must move in the same direction as the stabilator or elevator-like surface.

source.notes: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 6, states and illustrates that an antiservo tab moves in the same direction as the stabilator, making it less sensitive by opposing the force exerted by the pilot.

brief.student_must_understand: The stabilator and anti-servo tab deflect together in the same direction; the tab adds resistance/control feel rather than helping the surface move.
preserve: Anti-servo tab at the stabilator trailing edge
Increased control resistance and reduced sensitivity
refine: Use a clean side-view tail section
Make same-direction movement unmistakable
Keep the resistance cue secondary to the preflight movement check

visuals.mapping_reason: Each question asks how correct anti-balance/anti-servo tab operation is recognized; the source figure's same-direction motion is the exact answer relationship.

visual_inspection.review_note: The exact optimized 1600x1050 PNG and matching WebP were rendered and inspected against the locked Batch 1 quality standard. The all-moving stabilator, pivot, dashed neutral reference, and anti-servo tab are structurally clear; the two deflection arrows visibly point in the same direction, and the added-control-feel and reduced-sensitivity outcomes are legible without obscuring the preflight relationship.

visuals.concept: During spin autorotation the descending inner wing is more deeply stalled at the greater angle of attack while the rising outer wing is less stalled
visuals.reuse_justification: All four questions test the same autorotation asymmetry; the left-spin wording simply identifies the left wing as the descending inner wing.

source.notes: The FAA Airplane Flying Handbook glossary defines a spin as autorotation and states that the rising wing is less stalled than the descending wing, producing rolling, yawing and pitching motion. Chapter 5, Figure 5-15, independently identifies a spin as an aggravated stall and autorotation.

brief.student_must_understand: In a left spin, the left/inner wing descends and is more deeply stalled at the greater AoA; the right/outer wing rises and is less stalled.
preserve: Left wing as descending inner wing
Greater AoA and deeper stall on the inner wing
Outer wing rising and less stalled
refine: Use a credible front-oblique aircraft view where left and right cannot be confused
Show differential wing state without implying either wing produces normal unstalled lift
Keep the autorotation path subordinate to the wing comparison

visuals.mapping_reason: The questions all ask which wing is more stalled or at the greater AoA during autorotation; the visual isolates that exact inner-versus-outer wing state.

visual_inspection.review_note: The exact optimized 1600x1050 PNG and matching WebP were rendered and inspected against the locked Batch 1 quality standard. The corrected pilot-left wing is viewer-right, descending and more deeply stalled, while the pilot-right wing is viewer-left, rising and less stalled. Rotation, relative angle-of-attack cues, and inner/outer-wing labels are mutually consistent and readable.

visuals.concept: In the generic FAA spin-recovery sequence, full opposite rudder is applied before brisk forward elevator reduces angle of attack
visuals.reuse_justification: Both questions test the identical control-order relationship: rudder is applied before elevator during the generic spin-recovery sequence.

source.notes: The FAA Airplane Flying Handbook's six-step generic spin-recovery template places full opposite rudder at step 3 and positive brisk forward elevator immediately after it at step 4. The handbook explicitly requires aircraft-specific manufacturer procedures to take precedence.

brief.student_must_understand: After power idle and ailerons neutral, apply full rudder opposite the rotation, then immediately move the elevator briskly forward to reduce AoA; the question-specific answer is rudder before elevator.
preserve: Full opposite rudder before forward elevator
Elevator forward immediately after rudder application
refine: Emphasize steps 3 and 4 while retaining enough sequence context to avoid unsafe shorthand
Use conventional control icons or aircraft-control callouts
Make BEFORE visually unambiguous

visuals.mapping_reason: Both questions explicitly ask which control is used first; the FAA recovery template provides the exact rudder-before-elevator order with the required manufacturer-procedure caveat.

visual_inspection.review_note: The exact optimized 1600x1050 PNG and matching WebP were rendered and inspected against the locked Batch 1 quality standard. The complete six-step generic FAA sequence is readable, with full opposite rudder at step 3 visibly preceding forward elevator and angle-of-attack reduction at step 4. The POH/AFM precedence warning is prominent and the recovery is not presented as aircraft-universal.

visuals.concept: Extending trailing-edge flaps adds drag, reduces glide efficiency and maximum forward distance, and makes the power-off descent path steeper
visuals.reuse_justification: All eight questions test consequences of the same flap-in-glide relationship: added drag reduces L/D and forward range, so the glide steepens and rate of descent increases.

source.notes: The FAA Airplane Flying Handbook states that flap extension produces greater drag and permits a steeper descent angle; Figure 9-2 compares the resulting approach angles. FAA-H-8083-25C, Chapter 6, further states that flaps increase lift and induced drag and that later extension increases drag with little additional lift.

brief.student_must_understand: From the same starting height, the clean aircraft follows the shallower, longer best-glide path; flap extension adds drag, reduces L/D and range, and produces a steeper path with greater height loss per forward distance.
preserve: Same starting height for clean and flap configurations
Lower L/D and greater rate of descent with flaps
refine: Use a clean side-by-side or overlaid glide-path comparison
Show credible flap deflection on the flaps-down aircraft
Keep path geometry and labels readable at mobile size
add: CLEAN: higher L/D / longer glide cue
FLAPS DOWN: more drag / lower L/D cue

visuals.mapping_reason: Every selected question asks for the L/D, descent-angle, descent-rate, or maximum-distance consequence of flap extension in a glide; one clean-versus-flaps path comparison directly teaches the shared relationship.

visual_inspection.review_note: The exact optimized 1600x1050 PNG and matching WebP were rendered and inspected against the locked Batch 1 quality standard. The clean configuration follows the shallower, longer glide path, while the flaps-down configuration follows the steeper, shorter path; the main-wing-root flap cue, added-drag explanation, and reduced-glide-distance outcome agree and remain readable at application scale.
